item.title: When Everything Is a "Need," We Lose More Than Flexibility
item.description:
Leadership

When Everything Is a "Need," We Lose More Than Flexibility

There's a hidden cost for treating every preference like a nonnegotiable.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Most "needs" are actually preferences disguised as requirements, and the difference matters.
  • Framing preferences as needs narrows your own thinking and closes off real alternatives.
  • Rigid "needs" language makes colleagues feel there's no room to negotiate or push back.
  • Naming what matters and why leaves room for flexibility without losing your priorities.
Stop calling everything a "need"
Source: Ketut Subiyanto / Pexels

This article was co-authored with Miki Feldman Simon, MSc, PCC, an executive coach, speaker, and award-winning author who helps leaders turn insight into intentional action.

"I need 24 hours' notice."

"I need to talk to you right away."

"I need complete quiet to concentrate."

"I need to be in that meeting."

"I need an hour to exercise every day."

Most of us use the word need dozens of times a day. Sometimes those needs are real. As many of us learned from Abraham Maslow (and more contemporary researchers), we need shelter. We need sleep. We need food. We need safety. We need meaningful human connection.

Many of the things we describe as “needs” are actually the conditions under which we feel most comfortable or would ideally like things to happen. They may help us feel most satisfied or make things easier for us. But does that truly make them needs?

As executive coaches, we've spent decades helping leaders understand what they genuinely need to do their best work. Self-awareness includes knowing what helps you think clearly, perform well, recharge, and succeed. It also includes communicating those needs to others clearly and without apology.

At the same time, we've both noticed another pattern in our coaching: our clients stating (or sometimes demanding) “needs” that are, in reality, strong preferences. And like most things in psychology and leadership, the challenge often isn't one extreme or the other. It's finding the balance.

When every preference becomes a need, something shifts. We begin to create rigid constraints, both for ourselves and for the people around us. We've both seen clients become trapped by their own language, demands, and expectations. And it can become a self-defeating dynamic.

One client we worked with told herself (and everyone around her) that she needed 24 hours’ notice to make changes to client proposals. And in an ideal world, she would get that. But when an important client communicated to her team members that they wanted to make a change to a proposal with 8 hours of turnaround time, her colleagues felt trapped. Were they supposed to tell the client no? Were they supposed to keep this request from the leader? Were they going to stay silent? Her stated "need" unintentionally created hesitation and made the team believe there was no room for flexibility. It wasn't until a brave team member asked whether the 24-hour notice was truly nonnegotiable that the leader replied, "Of course we should make the change." What she had intended as the ideal working condition had been interpreted as an absolute rule.

article continues after advertisement

It’s not just our colleagues or clients who suffer a penalty when we confuse wants and needs. When a leader tells themself, "I need 24 hours' notice," their mind immediately closes the door to alternatives. If they have only six hours, they stop asking, "What can I realistically accomplish?" and start focusing on everything that's impossible.

When you say, "I need complete quiet to work," you may overlook other ways to create focus, even if they're not ideal.

When you tell yourself, "I need to be in that meeting," you may miss other opportunities to influence the decision before or after the meeting takes place.

The language of need can narrow our thinking. It creates a single acceptable path, making it harder to see options we might otherwise consider.

It can also affect our relationships.

When everything is communicated as a need, other people have little room to maneuver. Colleagues, partners, friends, and family may begin to experience us as inflexible because every request feels nonnegotiable. Collaboration becomes more difficult because there appears to be only one acceptable solution.

That doesn't mean we should stop communicating what matters to us.

Instead, it helps to become more precise.

Rather than saying, "I need 24 hours' notice," we might say, "Twenty-four hours works best because it gives me time to gather information and produce my best work. And if that’s not always possible, let me know, and we will see what we can figure out.”

article continues after advertisement

Instead of, "I need complete quiet," we might say, "What works best for me is a quiet space when I'm doing deep thinking."

Rather than, "I need to exercise for an hour every day," we might say, "Ideally, I like to exercise for an hour each day because I know I feel and function at my best when I do."

Notice what changed.

We didn't minimize what was important. We explained why it mattered while leaving room for conversation, creativity, and collaboration.

Perhaps even more importantly, we left room for ourselves.

When we describe everything as a need, we often create our own cage. We convince ourselves there is only one acceptable way forward. Preferences, on the other hand, invite problem-solving. They remind us that while one option may be ideal, it isn't necessarily the only path to success.

This distinction becomes especially valuable in leadership. Leaders constantly encounter changing priorities, limited resources, competing needs, and imperfect conditions. The ability to hold onto what matters while remaining flexible about how to achieve it is part of what makes people adaptable, resilient, and effective.

So the next time you catch yourself saying, "I need…", pause for a moment.

Ask yourself:

  • Is this truly a need, or is it a preference?

  • How else could I communicate what works best for me?

  • What other possibilities might I see if I left the door open just a little wider?

Sometimes changing a single word doesn't just change how others hear us.

It changes how much agency we give ourselves.
